TIJCEF Strengthens Evidence-Based Programming Through Monitoring and Impact Documentation

TIJCEF Strengthens Evidence-Based Programming Through Monitoring and Impact Documentation

The Tijwun Care and Empowerment Foundation (TIJCEF) is strengthening its approach to community development by placing programme documentation, beneficiary records and measurable results at the centre of how it tracks and communicates its interventions across communities.

The approach forms part of TIJCEF’s Evidence pillar, one of the four pillars guiding the Foundation’s work alongside Dignity, Agency and Resilience.

Rather than relying solely on statements about people being “empowered” or “impacted,” TIJCEF’s evidence approach focuses on documenting what interventions were implemented, where they took place, who participated, how many direct beneficiaries were reached and what programme records are available to support reported results.

The importance of this approach can already be seen across TIJCEF’s programme portfolio.

At Adroit International Academy in Yola, TIJCEF and Lead the Girl Foundation implemented a girls’ empowerment intervention reaching 200 girls.

At Government Girls College Yola, more than 400 girls participated in a STEM-focused outreach.

A youth empowerment seminar at Zion Centre in Girei reached 50 young people, while a women’s leadership and empowerment intervention in Taraba State reached 45 women.

These programme-level figures provide TIJCEF with something more valuable than general claims about community impact: identifiable records connecting beneficiaries to specific interventions.

From Activities to Verifiable Programme Records

Grassroots organisations frequently work in environments where immediate community needs take priority over sophisticated data systems.

A programme may be successfully conducted and photographed, but important information can be lost if beneficiary numbers, locations, dates, activities and outcomes are not properly recorded.

TIJCEF’s Evidence pillar seeks to address this challenge by treating documentation as part of programme implementation rather than an activity that begins only when an annual report or funding proposal is required.

This means evidence can begin with relatively simple records.

How many people attended?

Where did the programme take place?

Who were the implementing partners?

What group was targeted?

What activities were delivered?

What materials were provided?

What photographs, attendance records or participant feedback exist?

These questions help turn an activity into a documented intervention.

Programme Figures Show Different Levels of Reach

TIJCEF’s existing programme records illustrate why intervention-level documentation matters.

The Foundation should not simply combine every number into a large headline figure without retaining information about where those beneficiaries came from.

For example, the 200 girls reached at Adroit International Academy can be linked to a specific school-based girls’ empowerment programme jointly implemented with Lead the Girl Foundation.

The 400-plus girls reached at Government Girls College Yola belong to a different intervention focused on STEM exposure.

The 50 young people reached at Zion Centre, Girei, represent participants in a youth empowerment seminar.

The 45 women reached through the Taraba leadership and empowerment programme represent another distinct beneficiary group.

Separating these records allows TIJCEF to understand not only how many people it reaches but who it is reaching and through what type of intervention.

That is a more useful measure for programme management.

Evidence Prevents Double Counting

Maintaining programme-level records also helps prevent a common problem in development reporting: double counting.

A person may participate in more than one programme.

For example, an individual who attends a leadership programme could later volunteer during another TIJCEF intervention.

If every attendance is automatically counted as a unique beneficiary, the organisation’s cumulative reach could become inflated.

An evidence-based system should therefore distinguish between programme participations and unique beneficiaries wherever records make that possible.

The distinction becomes increasingly important as TIJCEF expands.

Programme participation tells the Foundation how much activity it has delivered.

Unique-beneficiary data provide a better indication of how many individual people have actually been reached.

Both measurements can be useful, but they answer different questions.

Evidence Also Means Acknowledging What Is Not Known

TIJCEF’s approach to evidence is equally important when programme information is incomplete.

The Foundation’s 2023 outreach to an orphanage in Katsina, for instance, can be documented through the visit by its Executive Director and the donation of gifts to children.

However, where a verified beneficiary figure is not available, an estimated number should not be introduced simply to make the programme appear larger.

Similarly, TIJCEF’s January 2026 two-day leadership training can be reported through its duration, programme records and participation of the President of Public Speakers Network of Africa Foundation alongside other resource persons.

Where the exact attendance figure has not been verified, it is more credible to leave that figure unstated than to estimate it.

This principle is central to evidence-based reporting:

What is not measured should not be presented as measured.

That standard protects both beneficiaries and the organisation.

Photographs Form Part of the Evidence Base

Programme photography also plays an important role in TIJCEF’s documentation.

Images from training sessions, school programmes and community activities provide visual records showing how interventions were implemented.

They can document participation, programme settings, organisational branding and engagement between volunteers, resource persons and beneficiaries.

But photographs have limitations.

A photograph showing a crowded training hall cannot independently establish that 100 people attended.

A photograph of smiling participants cannot prove that their income increased.

A picture of students during a STEM outreach cannot establish that they subsequently pursued STEM careers.

Photography therefore supports evidence but does not replace beneficiary records or outcome measurement.

This distinction enables TIJCEF to use visual documentation responsibly.

Beneficiary Numbers Are Outputs, Not Automatically Impact

One of the most important elements of the Evidence pillar is distinguishing between outputs and outcomes.

Reaching 400 girls is an output.

Showing that those girls increased their STEM knowledge would be an outcome.

Training 50 young people is an output.

Showing that participants subsequently applied specific skills would represent a further result.

Reaching 45 women through leadership programming is an output.

Demonstrating increased participation in leadership or livelihood activities would require additional evidence.

This distinction prevents programme reach from automatically being described as transformation.

TIJCEF can celebrate beneficiary numbers while remaining accurate about what those figures actually demonstrate.

Evidence Supports Sustainable Development

TIJCEF’s approach also connects with the wider international emphasis on data in sustainable development.

The United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal framework relies heavily on indicators because progress cannot be assessed effectively without reliable information.

SDG 17, for example, includes targets related to increasing the availability of high-quality, timely and reliable data for sustainable development. United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 17⁠�

For a grassroots organisation, this does not require building a national statistical system.

It begins with ensuring that programme information is recorded consistently.

A reliable attendance sheet is evidence.

A properly completed beneficiary questionnaire is evidence.

A dated programme photograph is evidence.

A partner confirmation is evidence.

A pre- and post-programme assessment can provide evidence of change.

A follow-up interview can provide evidence about what happened after an intervention.

When combined systematically, these records create an increasingly strong picture of organisational performance.

Evidence Strengthens Accountability to Partners

Good programme data are also important for partnerships and fundraising.

Potential donors and institutional partners increasingly expect organisations to demonstrate what they have previously implemented.

An organisation able to provide programme dates, locations, beneficiary numbers, photographs, partners and measurable results is better positioned to demonstrate institutional capacity than one relying exclusively on broad statements.

For TIJCEF, this means its programme history can become part of its organisational evidence base.

The Adroit intervention demonstrates collaboration with another foundation.

The Government Girls College programme demonstrates large-scale school engagement.

The Girei seminar demonstrates youth-focused programming.

The Taraba intervention provides evidence of women-focused engagement.

The volunteer training demonstrates investment in internal capacity.

And the Katsina outreach documents humanitarian engagement with vulnerable children.

Together, these interventions begin to establish a traceable record of what the Foundation has done.

Evidence Must Protect Beneficiaries

Collecting information also creates responsibilities.

TIJCEF’s programmes involve groups including children and young people, meaning data collection must respect privacy, dignity and safeguarding principles.

Not every piece of information collected should be published.

Beneficiary names, contact information and sensitive personal details should be handled carefully.

Public impact reporting can rely primarily on aggregated information.

Instead of identifying individual children, TIJCEF can report that 200 girls participated in a programme.

Instead of publishing private questionnaire responses, results can be presented as aggregated percentages where appropriate.

This allows evidence to strengthen accountability without compromising beneficiary dignity.

Building a Culture of Evidence

TIJCEF’s Evidence pillar ultimately goes beyond numbers.

It represents an organisational culture in which claims are expected to have supporting records.

That means being willing to report both achievements and limitations.

It means distinguishing between direct beneficiaries and estimated reach.

It means recognising partners rather than claiming collaborative programmes as exclusively TIJCEF interventions.

It means acknowledging when a beneficiary number is unavailable.

And it means avoiding impressive-looking percentages that have no underlying dataset.

For a growing grassroots organisation, these practices can become important institutional strengths.

TIJCEF’s programmes already provide the foundation.

There are documented interventions involving 200 girls at Adroit International Academy, more than 400 girls at Government Girls College Yola, 50 young people in Girei and 45 women in Taraba, alongside other activities for which different forms of programme evidence exist.

The task of the Evidence pillar is to ensure that those activities become more than memories or photographs.

They become records.

Those records become data.

And where appropriate measurement exists, that data can eventually demonstrate outcomes.

For TIJCEF, this is what evidence-based community development means: not merely saying that impact happened, but building the records capable of showing what was done, who was reached and what changed.
